edition.deck: A deadly strike in Ukraine, a US election-day court ruling and new pressure on European security systems lead the latest developments.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritises overnight developments and fresh reporting. Returning stories are included only where the gather adds a significant development or materially new reporting.

content.headline: Russian bombing kills 26 at Ukrainian aid centre, officials say
content.shortHeadline: Russian strike kills 26 at Ukraine aid centre
content.standfirst: Officials say bombs hit a school shelter and aid distribution site in Komyshuvakha. Rescue work was interrupted by further drone attacks, and Russia has not publicly commented.

image.caption: Rescue crews work at the site of the strike in Komyshuvakha.

sources.originalTitle: Russian bombing kills 26 people at Ukraine aid centre, Kyiv says
Russian bombing of Ukrainian aid centre kills at least 26, Kyiv says

segments.body: At least 26 people were killed and five injured when Russian bombs hit an aid distribution centre in Komyshuvakha, in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region, Ukrainian officials say. The school was being used to distribute humanitarian aid and shelter residents. Officials initially reported 27 people missing.

segments.title: Rescue work and the wider war
segments.body: Rescue teams searched the rubble, but local officials said Russian drone attacks in the area forced them to stop several times. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the attack showed Moscow did not want de-escalation; Russia’s military has not publicly responded to the reports.

content.headline: US Supreme Court rejects Trump bid to set aside California ballots
content.shortHeadline: Supreme Court rejects Trump bid to set aside California ballots
content.standfirst: The ruling leaves in place lower-court decisions against separating about 20,000 ballots the Justice Department said might belong to non-citizens. California officials questioned the accuracy of the government’s list.

image.caption: Voters cast ballots in California.

sources.originalTitle: Supreme Court rejects Trump's request to stop California counting disputed votes
Supreme court rules against Trump over bid to force California to set aside ballots
Trump’s DoJ charges six more people in ‘voter fraud’ crackdown in California

segments.body: The US Supreme Court rejected the Trump administration’s request to set aside about 20,000 California ballots it alleged may have been issued to non-citizens. The court gave no explanation for its one-line order, which leaves lower-court rulings in place.

segments.title: Dispute over the voter list
segments.body: California election officials said the list supplied by the Justice Department contained inaccuracies and that separating ballots during voting risked excluding eligible voters. The department did not provide the underlying evidence or method for its claims, according to the Guardian’s account. Separately, federal prosecutors announced charges against six lawful permanent residents; the complaints allege false statements on naturalisation applications, not charges of voting fraud.

perspectives.body: California officials and voting-rights groups said the government had not disclosed how it identified the names and challenged the list’s reliability. The Supreme Court did not explain its decision.

content.headline: US officials report strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island as talks continue
content.shortHeadline: US officials report strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island
content.standfirst: US officials described the reported attacks as limited and defensive, but Washington has not publicly confirmed them. Iranian state media reported explosions as both countries signalled openness to negotiations.

image.caption: The coast of Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz.

sources.originalTitle: US strikes Iran ahead of midterm elections
US reportedly strikes Iran’s Qeshm Island as Vance voices optimism about a deal

segments.body: US officials told CBS that the United States struck Iran’s Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, describing the action as limited and defensive after the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps fired on a US aircraft. Iran’s state news agency reported explosions on the island, but described their cause as unclear. US Central Command had not responded to the BBC’s request for comment.

The reports came on the eve of US midterm elections and amid indirect efforts to end the war. Iran’s foreign minister said intensive talks were under way through mediators; Vice-President JD Vance said the US saw progress, while Donald Trump said there was no rush to escalate. The gathered reports do not establish the full scope or outcome of the reported strikes.

content.headline: Cyber-attacks disrupt supermarket freezers in seven European countries
content.shortHeadline: Cyber-attacks disrupt supermarket freezers across Europe
content.standfirst: Refrigeration systems in shops across seven countries were accessed remotely, with food spoiled in some stores. Who was responsible—and whether the incidents are linked to earlier attacks—remains unknown.

image.caption: Empty refrigerators at a supermarket after a reported IT incident.

sources.originalTitle: Shop freezers in seven European countries hit by cyber-attack
Who is hacking Europe’s supermarket fridges and freezers, and why?
Sådan kan hackere overtage styringen af et køleanlæg
If hackers can take control of a supermarket freezer, how vulnerable is other tech?
Sinister new Russian threat to the UK could turn supermarket freezers up to 55°C

segments.body: Dozens of supermarkets and smaller shops in seven European countries reported refrigeration problems after a cyber-attack. The systems were switched into defrost mode, allowing temperatures to rise; some freezers reportedly reached 50°C. Some retailers reported spoiled food, while others said they contained the disruption and kept stores open.

segments.title: Who is responsible remains unclear
segments.body: No group has claimed responsibility, and the gathered reporting does not establish who carried out the attacks or whether they are connected to earlier incidents in France or at US military sites. Experts say internet-connected refrigeration controls can be left without updates; a Danish cybersecurity expert cited by DR said the specific method used in these attacks is not known. The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre said it was working with partners and industry.

perspectives.body: A Danish cybersecurity expert told DR that remote access, software flaws or weak access controls can create vulnerabilities, but said investigators do not yet know how access was gained in these attacks.

content.headline: European troops rehearse possible Ukraine deployment as peace talks loom
content.shortHeadline: European troops rehearse a possible Ukraine mission
content.standfirst: Britain and France will lead an exercise in Poland for a multinational force that officials say would deploy only after a peace deal. US-mediated talks between Ukraine and Russia are also due next week.

image.caption: A British paratrooper takes part in a previous Nato training exercise in Finland.

sources.originalTitle: Thousands of European troops to rehearse Ukraine deployment in event of peace
Ukraine war briefing: US to mediate talks with Kyiv and Moscow in Abu Dhabi next week, says Witkoff
USA skal mægle mellem Rusland og Ukraine i Abu Dhabi i næste uge

segments.body: Nearly 2,800 troops will rehearse how a multinational force could deploy to Ukraine if a peace deal is reached. The exercise, led by Britain and France, is scheduled for 9–22 November in Poland and will test movement, supply and coordination across land, sea and air. The BBC says 12 European nations will take part; the Guardian describes forces from 10 countries.

segments.title: Plans depend on a ceasefire
segments.body: Western officials say the force would not take part in offensive operations, peacekeeping or ceasefire monitoring, and would be deployed only after fighting stops. Its final size and rules of engagement remain unsettled. US, Ukrainian and Russian delegations are due to meet in Abu Dhabi on 10 and 11 November, with post-war security, de-escalation and humanitarian issues on the agenda.

content.headline: US midterm campaign spending projected to reach nearly $12bn
content.shortHeadline: US midterm campaign spending nears $12bn
content.standfirst: The election campaign is projected to be the most expensive midterm cycle on record, with outside groups responsible for more than half of spending reported so far. Final totals will not be available until after voting.

sources.originalTitle: US midterms campaign 'shattering' spending records to be most expensive ever

segments.body: The 2026 US midterm campaign is projected to cost $11.9bn, about 30% more than the 2022 midterms, according to OpenSecrets estimates reported by the BBC. Federal filings showed more than $9.5bn spent by mid-October, with political action committees and Super PACs accounting for about $5.5bn.

Billionaire Elon Musk was the largest individual donor, giving almost half a billion dollars, much of it to groups supporting Republican candidates. Most campaign money went to advertising, according to ad-tracking figures cited by the BBC. The projected total is not a final count; full spending reports are due after the election.

content.headline: Indonesia’s wildfire haze tests ties with Singapore and Malaysia
content.shortHeadline: Indonesia’s wildfire haze strains ties with neighbours
content.standfirst: Weeks of smoke from Indonesian fires have brought health complaints and political pressure in Singapore and Malaysia. Governments are balancing public anger with the risks of confrontation and the limits of regional agreements.

image.caption: Smoke from Indonesian wildfires has drifted into Singapore and Malaysia.

sources.originalTitle: Indonesia's toxic haze is giving its neighbours a political headache

segments.body: Smoke from wildfires in Indonesia’s Kalimantan, Papua and Sumatra regions has drifted into Singapore and Malaysia, contributing to respiratory illness and headaches. This year’s fires have been harder to contain amid drought conditions worsened by a strong El Niño, according to the BBC.

segments.title: Diplomacy under pressure
segments.body: Singapore has set up haze shelters, distributed masks to vulnerable residents and is investigating 10 Singapore-registered companies for possible links to fires. Malaysia has ruled out a formal protest and is exploring a prevention agreement with Indonesia. The regional haze accord has no power to punish companies or compel governments to act, critics say.

content.headline: UK and EU draft deal would remove checks on food exports
content.shortHeadline: UK and EU draft deal would cut food-export checks
content.standfirst: A proposed agreement would remove many post-Brexit certificates, inspections and fees for agricultural trade. The draft still needs discussion with EU member states ahead of a UK-EU summit later this month.

sources.originalTitle: UK and EU agree draft deal to scrap Brexit red tape over food exports

segments.body: The UK and EU have agreed a draft sanitary and phytosanitary deal that would remove many checks and fees on food and agricultural exports. The government says the changes could eventually bring the UK economy £5.1bn in annual benefits; the draft has been circulated to EU countries for consideration, not yet approved.

segments.title: Standards and remaining negotiations
segments.body: The proposal would allow some exports, including fresh sausages, shellfish from domestic waters and seed potatoes, to resume, and would permit UK pets to travel to the EU using pet passports. In return, the UK would align with relevant EU rules on plant, animal and food standards. EU ambassadors are due to discuss the draft, while other parts of the wider reset remain under negotiation.

content.headline: UK cyber agency warns AI malware could target critical infrastructure
content.shortHeadline: UK cyber agency warns AI malware could hit infrastructure
content.standfirst: The National Cyber Security Centre says it is highly likely that AI-powered malware will be used in a ransomware attack on UK critical infrastructure by 2028, as attackers use the technology to find weaknesses and write code.

sources.originalTitle: AI-powered malware ‘highly likely’ to be used to hack UK infrastructure by 2028

segments.body: The National Cyber Security Centre says it is highly likely that AI-powered malware will be used in a ransomware attack on UK critical national infrastructure between now and 2028. The warning covers sectors including energy, transport, food, health and finance, and appears in the agency’s annual review.

segments.title: A growing risk
segments.body: The agency says AI could help attackers scout targets, locate weaknesses and write malicious code. Its chief executive is due to warn that the coming months could bring an unprecedented rise in cyber incidents. The review also says Russia and China are expected to use AI routinely in cyber-attacks; it does not attribute the separate supermarket freezer incidents to either country.

content.headline: Trial opens for nine men accused of offences against drugged woman
content.shortHeadline: Nine men deny offences in trial over abuse of drugged woman
content.standfirst: Prosecutors told a Manchester court that a woman’s husband secretly abused her for years and invited other men to join. He has pleaded guilty to offences against her; nine others deny charges, and the trial is continuing.

sources.originalTitle: The nine men accused of sex offences against woman drugged and raped by her husband

segments.body: The trial of nine men accused of offences against a woman who prosecutors say was drugged and sexually abused has opened at Manchester’s Minshull Street Crown Court. Her husband, who cannot be named to protect her anonymity, has pleaded guilty to 62 offences against her. The nine defendants deny charges including rape and conspiracy to rape.

segments.title: Evidence before the jury
segments.body: Prosecutor Louise Oakley told the jury police found more than a million images and videos on the husband’s phone. The jury will have to consider whether the woman was unconscious or pretending to be, the court heard. The trial is expected to last at least six weeks; the allegations against the nine defendants have not been determined.

content.headline: Millions of UK landline users face digital switchover by January 2027
content.shortHeadline: One million UK households still need digital landlines
content.standfirst: The old copper-wire network is due to close in January, but about one million households and businesses have yet to switch. Campaigners warn power cuts and poor mobile coverage could leave vulnerable people without a reliable way to call for help.

sources.originalTitle: The millions of people who face losing their landline phone in digital switchover

segments.body: Openreach says roughly one million households and businesses have yet to move from traditional copper landlines to internet-based phone connections ahead of the planned 31 January 2027 shutdown. A failed or delayed upgrade could leave customers without a working phone or moved to a temporary service with fewer features.

segments.title: Power cuts and vulnerable customers
segments.body: Unlike conventional landlines, digital phones rely on mains electricity, raising concerns for people in remote areas and those who depend on telecare alarms. Telecoms firms have supplied some vulnerable customers with backup batteries, but a campaigner says they may not be enough during prolonged outages. Ofcom says it is monitoring the change and has fined one firm over risks to vulnerable customers.

content.headline: Burnham to ask Commonwealth countries to help shape slavery apology
content.shortHeadline: Burnham to invite Commonwealth input on slavery apology
content.standfirst: The prime minister plans to begin a structured dialogue at the Antigua and Barbuda summit about a possible formal apology for Britain’s role in the slave trade. Downing Street has ruled out reparations.

image.caption: Andy Burnham is due to begin talks on a possible formal apology at the Commonwealth summit.

sources.originalTitle: PM to ask countries affected by UK’s role in slavery to help shape formal apology

segments.body: Andy Burnham is expected to invite countries affected by Britain’s role in the transatlantic slave trade to help shape a possible formal apology. Downing Street says he will launch a structured dialogue at the Commonwealth summit in Antigua and Barbuda, which begins on Tuesday. No decision on the form of an apology has been announced.

segments.title: What the government has said
segments.body: The government has ruled out reparations, while Burnham is expected to discuss debt restructuring for countries facing higher borrowing costs. Officials at the summit said other Commonwealth countries had responded positively to the proposed dialogue. The government says affected countries should help shape any apology rather than Britain deciding its terms unilaterally.

content.headline: DR finds 82 videos of Danish children being beaten or humiliated
content.shortHeadline: DR identifies 82 videos of violence against Danish children
content.standfirst: A three-month review found videos on social media showing Danish children and teenagers being assaulted or humiliated. Experts say sharing can extend conflicts, but the material does not establish how common the behaviour is overall.

image.caption: Anna Sørine Bukh has spoken about her son Elias’s death and the videos shared online.

sources.originalTitle: 'Kys min sko': Børn bruger ydmygelsesvideoer som våben mod hinanden
Før og efter drabet på 15-årig dreng blev voldsomme videoer delt online
'Det vigtigste, I kan lære din søn, er, at han altid kan komme til jer': Læs eksperternes svar om voldsvideoer blandt børn

segments.body: A company working for DR identified 82 videos of Danish children and young people being beaten or humiliated on TikTok, Snapchat and Telegram during a three-month period. Some videos had tens of thousands of views; a number exceeded 100,000. The review is a count of material found, not a measure of how widespread such violence is among young people.

segments.title: Conflict can continue online
segments.body: Experts told DR that some videos follow disputes among children and teenagers and can be used to shame or threaten others, extending the conflict after the event. In a separate account, the mother of Elias, who was killed by a childhood friend at 15, said humiliating videos circulated before and after his death. She said she does not believe one video caused the killing.

segments.title: How adults can respond
segments.body: A child-safety adviser told DR that adults should listen without rushing to punish or take away a child’s phone, and seek help from the school, police or Red Barnet’s SletDet service when needed. Experts said children should be able to ask adults for help if they encounter violent material.

content.headline: South Greenland police report fewer calls after alcohol ban
content.shortHeadline: South Greenland police report quieter weekend after alcohol ban
content.standfirst: Police in South Greenland say they received no calls for an entire 24-hour period over a payday weekend, when reports normally rise. The district chief says the ban has freed officers for other work, though unreported incidents remain unknown.

image.caption: South Greenland police district chief Michael Karstenskov says officers received no calls for 24 hours.

sources.originalTitle: Nul drinks og nul anmeldelser: Politi i Sydgrønland kalder lønnings-fredag ’bemærkelsesværdig rolig’

segments.body: South Greenland police say reports have fallen in the weeks since the municipality introduced an alcohol ban a month ago, following a killing involving alcohol. District chief Michael Karstenskov called the latest payday weekend unusually quiet: officers received no calls for a full 24 hours.

Karstenskov said the quieter period has allowed police to complete pending cases and increase prevention work with schools, including discussions about hard drugs. He cautioned that police cannot guarantee people are not drinking at home or that every incident is reported; his assessment is based on calls and officers’ contact with residents.

content.headline: Copenhagen and Herning compete to host future handball championships
content.shortHeadline: Copenhagen and Herning vie for handball championships
content.standfirst: Danish Handball is considering which city should host the men’s 2031 World Championship and women’s 2032 European Championship. Copenhagen has set aside event funding; Herning says the tournaments bring visitors and business to the city.

image.caption: Jyske Bank Boxen in Herning has hosted eight handball championships since 2010.

sources.originalTitle: Kampen om klappepølserne: København og Herning dyster om håndboldslutrunder

segments.body: Copenhagen and Herning are competing to host the men’s 2031 World Championship and women’s 2032 European Championship. Danish Handball’s board is discussing the choice, with a decision expected to be announced Tuesday or Wednesday if one is made. The federation has previously said Copenhagen is its first choice and Herning its second.

segments.title: Different benefits for the host cities
segments.body: A DR handball analyst said Copenhagen could offer commercial advantages and attract sponsors. Herning’s city centre chief said championship visitors benefit businesses across the city, not just the arena. Copenhagen has reserved DKK 26m from its major-events fund to support hosting the tournaments.

content.headline: Finland’s president defends call with Putin after Danish criticism
content.shortHeadline: Stubb defends Putin call after Frederiksen’s criticism
content.standfirst: Alexander Stubb says the call was intended to deter escalation and was made at Ukraine’s request ahead of planned talks. A Finnish analyst, however, says it exposed divisions over Europe’s place in negotiations.

image.caption: Finnish President Alexander Stubb defended his call with Vladimir Putin.

sources.originalTitle: I sidste uge ringede Finlands præsident til Putin. Nu forklarer han, hvorfor den ombruste samtale var vigtig

segments.body: Finnish President Alexander Stubb defended his recent 90-minute call with Vladimir Putin, saying it was not a sign of weakness or a softening of Finland’s support for Ukraine. He said he and Norway’s prime minister delivered a firm message intended to discourage escalation, and that the call followed a request from Ukraine ahead of planned talks.

segments.title: Disagreement over the approach
segments.body: Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen has questioned what the call could achieve while Putin does not want peace. A Finnish foreign-policy analyst said the contact risked highlighting Nordic and European divisions and did not secure Europe a place in negotiations. Another security analyst cautioned against overstating the effect, saying support for Ukraine and pressure on Russia remained unchanged.

content.headline: Everton deepen Newcastle crisis as Barry keeps scoring and Grealish remains out
content.shortHeadline: Everton deepen Newcastle crisis; Barry scores again
content.standfirst: Everton’s 1-0 win at St James’ Park lifted them to seventh and left Newcastle with a fourth defeat in six league games. Thierno Barry scored again, while Jack Grealish’s return remains unclear.

sources.originalTitle: Jeers again as home woes continue - Jaissle has big problems at Newcastle
From nightmare debut season to Everton hero - Barry's revival
Grealish can still have Everton future - Moyes

segments.body: Everton won 1-0 at Newcastle to move into seventh. A goalkeeping error gave Thierno Barry the only goal, while substitute Jacob Ramsey was sent off. Newcastle were booed at full-time after a fourth defeat in six Premier League games.

segments.title: Barry’s turnaround
segments.body: Barry has matched last season’s eight-goal total in 12 games, after needing 41 appearances to reach that mark. He scored against Newcastle for the second time in five days and has eight goals in all competitions this season; only Erling Haaland has more among Premier League players, according to the report.

segments.title: Grealish’s status remains unclear
segments.body: Grealish missed both Newcastle wins after a disciplinary issue and was also described by Everton as unavailable because of fitness. David Moyes said there was a way back for the midfielder but did not say when he might return, or whether the disciplinary matter was resolved.

content.headline: Carrick says United can change their season as winless run reaches nine
content.shortHeadline: Carrick says United can change course after nine games without a win
content.standfirst: Manchester United manager Michael Carrick says he is focused on turning the season around, despite a run of nine games without a win and growing speculation over his future.

sources.originalTitle: Carrick says it's 'crazy' but he's looking forward to Roma game

segments.body: United go into their next match on a nine-game winless run in all competitions, their worst such spell since 1988-89. They are 17th in the Premier League and 21st in the Champions League table after three games. Carrick said he could not predict what would happen to him but was looking forward to the chance to change the season’s direction.

segments.title: Mainoo backs the squad
segments.body: Kobbie Mainoo, who returned from a muscular injury as a substitute at Chelsea, said the team were one win away from changing the season. He acknowledged the results had been poor and said United’s current position was unacceptable for a club of their size.

content.headline: Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel in intensive care after serious injury
content.shortHeadline: Tenerife striker De Miguel in intensive care after serious injury
content.standfirst: Jesus de Miguel is in a stable condition in intensive care after a collision during Tenerife’s match against Andorra. Spanish media reported he suffered a cardiac arrest in the ambulance and was resuscitated.

sources.originalTitle: Tenerife player in intensive care with injury

segments.body: Tenerife said the 30-year-old striker was admitted to hospital and was “stable despite the severity of his condition”. Spanish media, including Marca, reported that he suffered a cardiac arrest in the ambulance and was resuscitated by paramedics. The club’s statement did not give further details of his injuries.

segments.title: Match abandoned
segments.body: The incident happened in stoppage time, when Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono collided with De Miguel while moving to clear a long ball. Medical staff treated the motionless player on the pitch; the referee sent Owono off and abandoned the match, which was tied 2-2.

content.headline: Sunderland back Le Bris despite bottom-place start and sharp decline
content.shortHeadline: Sunderland back Le Bris as club seek to halt slide
content.standfirst: Sunderland’s first nine league games have left them bottom, but club sources say they believe manager Regis le Bris can improve results. The team’s defensive decline and missed chances help explain the concern.

image.caption: Regis le Bris was appointed Sunderland manager in June 2024.

sources.originalTitle: Bottom club Sunderland to stick with manager Le Bris

segments.body: Sunderland have one win from their first nine league games and are bottom of the Premier League. Club sources told BBC Sport they believe Le Bris can turn results around. He led the club to promotion and then seventh place last season, but that strong campaign has given way to a difficult start.

segments.title: A change at both ends
segments.body: Sunderland’s defensive numbers have worsened: opponents’ average expected goals per shot have risen from the league’s second-lowest to its second-highest, while goalkeeper Robin Roefs has a 50% save rate, the lowest in the division. At the other end, Sunderland rank 10th for expected goals but have scored six fewer than expected.

content.headline: Fifa will let council members inspect documents on World Cup sell-off plan
content.shortHeadline: Fifa offers council members limited access to World Cup sell-off files
content.standfirst: Fifa says council members can inspect key documents on its abandoned World Cup investment proposal, but only in person in Zurich and under confidentiality rules. Which documents will be available is unclear.

sources.originalTitle: Fifa to share 'key documents' over World Cup sell-off plan

segments.body: Fifa council members will be able to view “key documents” on the abandoned Fifa Forward Enterprise proposal at the organisation’s Zurich headquarters. Secretary general Mattias Grafstrom said access would be subject to “strict review protocols to preserve confidentiality”. Fifa has not specified which documents will be made available.

segments.title: Uefa wants answers
segments.body: Uefa had set Fifa a deadline of 2 November to provide information and answer more than 100 questions about the proposal and its governance. Fifa said the questions exceeded what its administration could reasonably have anticipated and that it was working on a response. Uefa has said earlier answers left fundamental questions unresolved.

content.headline: England call up Spencer and Randall after injuries to scrum-halves
content.shortHeadline: England add Spencer and Randall after scrum-half injuries
content.standfirst: Ben Spencer and Harry Randall join England’s squad for the Nations Championship after injuries ruled out Alex Mitchell and Archie McParland. Mitchell is awaiting a scan on his hamstring.

sources.originalTitle: England call up Spencer and Randall as injuries hit

segments.body: England have added Ben Spencer and Harry Randall after Northampton scrum-halves Alex Mitchell and Archie McParland were ruled out with injuries. Mitchell suffered a hamstring problem in Saturday’s match and was due to have a scan; McParland has a calf injury.

segments.title: Other selection questions
segments.body: Jack van Poortvliet, who started England’s three summer Tests, appears set to remain first choice at scrum-half. First-choice fly-half Fin Smith is also struggling with a calf problem, leaving Marcus Smith and George Ford in contention to cover if needed.

content.headline: Australia rest Cummins, Hazlewood and Starc for England white-ball series
content.shortHeadline: Australia leave out pace trio for England white-ball series
content.standfirst: Australia have rested Pat Cummins, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Starc from the upcoming ODI series against England after their recent Test campaign. Cummins and Hazlewood will also miss the T20s.

image.caption: Josh Hazlewood, Pat Cummins and Mitchell Starc, who won the 2023 ODI World Cup with Australia.

sources.originalTitle: Australia omit star pace trio for England series

segments.body: Australia will be without Cummins, Hazlewood and Starc for the three-match ODI series against England. Cummins and Hazlewood are also omitted from the five-match T20 squad; Starc has retired from the format. The veteran seamers played all three Tests in Australia’s recent series loss to South Africa.

segments.title: New options in the squads
segments.body: Mahli Beardman, 21, is included in both squads and could make his ODI debut. Uncapped wicketkeepers Sam Harper and Lachlan Shaw are named for the T20s. Mitchell Marsh will again captain the ODI side while Cummins, who remains its formal captain, has played only one 50-over match since November 2024.

content.headline: Shelton brings in Alcaraz’s former coach Ferrero to help challenge at majors
content.shortHeadline: Shelton teams up with former Alcaraz coach Ferrero
content.standfirst: Ben Shelton is joining forces with Juan Carlos Ferrero, who coached Carlos Alcaraz to six Grand Slam titles. The partnership is aimed at helping the US Open runner-up improve his consistency at the top level.

image.caption: Juan Carlos Ferrero helped Carlos Alcaraz win six Grand Slam titles before they split at the end of 2025.

sources.originalTitle: Can Alcaraz's ex-coach help Shelton challenge his former protege?

segments.body: Shelton, the world number four and US Open runner-up, will work with former world number one Juan Carlos Ferrero, who helped Alcaraz win six Grand Slam titles before their split at the end of 2025. The pair are due to begin formal work in an off-season training block in the United States.

segments.title: What Shelton still needs
segments.body: The BBC analysis points to Shelton’s improved backhand and defence at the US Open, but says his forehand let him down in key moments of the final. It also notes a recent defeat by world number 222 Jerome Kym in Basel as a reminder of the consistency he still needs to find.

content.headline: Juan Atkins, Detroit techno pioneer and Belleville Three member, dies at 64
content.shortHeadline: Juan Atkins, Detroit techno pioneer, dies at 64
content.standfirst: As Model 500 and one half of Cybotron, Atkins helped shape a sound that travelled far beyond Detroit. His influence reaches from the Belleville Three to artists who sampled his music decades later.

image.caption: Juan Atkins, a pioneer of Detroit techno.

sources.originalTitle: Juan Atkins, pioneer of Detroit techno sound, dies aged 64

segments.body: Juan Atkins, a founding figure of Detroit techno, has died aged 64. His agency told Resident Advisor that he was found unresponsive in a Mexico City hotel before a performance and was pronounced dead at hospital; no cause of death was given.

segments.title: A sound that travelled
segments.body: With Richard Davis in Cybotron, and later as Model 500, Atkins made electronic music that joined dancefloor drive to science-fiction imagery. He also founded Metroplex, a label that released his work and music by other Detroit artists. His track “Clear” has been sampled widely, including by Missy Elliott on “Lose Control.”

content.headline: Bad Brains revisit the raw beginnings of their punk legacy
content.shortHeadline: Bad Brains revisit their explosive first recordings
content.standfirst: The band’s newly remastered 1979 studio demo captures the force that made them punk legends. Their history also holds serious contradictions, including homophobic abuse and a song later condemned by the group.

image.caption: HR performing with Bad Brains at Wetlands in New York in 1999.

sources.originalTitle: ‘They said we incited riots’: explosive punks Bad Brains on drugs, self-destruction and recording from jail

segments.body: Bad Brains’ first studio session, recorded in 1979, has been remastered and released as Are You Ready: The First Studio Recording. The six-track demo preserves the speed and intensity that helped the Washington DC band become a defining force in American hardcore.

segments.title: A legacy with a shadow
segments.body: The band’s early years brought bans from Washington venues and a notorious failed attempt to enter the UK without work papers. Their influence is clear, but so are the harms in their history: the reporting recalls homophobic clashes with members of the hardcore scene and the widely condemned 1989 song “Don’t Blow Bubbles,” which the band later disowned.

content.headline: Mal Evans’s Beatles memoir brings his account of meeting Elvis to print
content.shortHeadline: Mal Evans’s Beatles memoir is to be published
content.standfirst: The road manager’s 95,000-word account, assembled from recordings and family archives, is due in December. It includes his recollections of the Beatles meeting Elvis Presley and their dangerous 1966 trip to the Philippines.

image.caption: Mal Evans with Paul McCartney and George Harrison at the Hollywood Bowl in August 1965.

sources.originalTitle: Meeting Elvis was ‘my biggest day with the Beatles’, says road manager’s book

segments.body: Mal Evans, the Beatles’ road manager and early archivist, recorded a memoir in 1975 but died before it could be published. With the Beatles will appear for the first time in December, edited by Beatles scholar Kenneth Womack from Evans’s dictated recordings and material preserved by his family.

segments.title: A witness to the band’s history
segments.body: Evans describes the group’s 1965 meeting with Elvis Presley as the biggest day of his years with the Beatles. His account also follows the band through the Philippines in 1966, where he recalls being threatened at gunpoint and the group being jostled at the airport after an unintended slight to Imelda Marcos.

content.headline: Steve Ellis, singer of Love Affair’s “Everlasting Love”, dies at 76
content.shortHeadline: Love Affair singer Steve Ellis dies aged 76
content.standfirst: Ellis fronted the group behind the 1968 UK chart-topper “Everlasting Love” and went on to work with Paul Weller. The singer’s death was announced after complications from a chronic illness.

image.caption: Steve Ellis in 1982.

sources.originalTitle: Steve Ellis, frontman of Everlasting Love hitmakers Love Affair, dies aged 76

segments.body: Steve Ellis, frontman of 1960s pop-rock band Love Affair, has died aged 76. A social media message said he died peacefully on 30 October after complications from a chronic illness; it did not name the illness.

segments.title: A song that endured
segments.body: Ellis sang Love Affair’s version of “Everlasting Love,” which spent two weeks at No 1 in the UK in 1968. After the band’s run of hits, he pursued other groups and a solo career. His later collaboration with Paul Weller included several co-written songs, most recently on Ellis’s album Baby Faced Assassin, released in September.

content.headline: Underscores says Gen Z is not a loveless generation
content.shortHeadline: Underscores on love songs and a leap to bigger stages
content.standfirst: After years in the experimental pop underground, April Grey’s album U has brought her to larger audiences and a place on Charli xcx’s tour. She talks about learning to write love songs and adjusting to arena-sized shows.

image.caption: Underscores, also known as April Grey.

sources.originalTitle: Pop prodigy Underscores: ‘I don’t think Gen Z is a loveless generation’

segments.body: April Grey, who records as Underscores, describes U as a deliberate move towards pop after her previous album, Wallsocket, left her feeling misunderstood. The record’s nine love songs pushed her to explore a subject she had struggled to connect with, though she rejects the idea that Gen Z has little love to give.

segments.title: A new scale
segments.body: The release has helped move Grey from upgraded headline shows to supporting Charli xcx on an arena tour. She says the challenge is adapting her performance to sharply different room sizes, and that meeting childhood hero Skrillex recently made the scale of her own rise feel real.

content.headline: Ashe’s new album turns a comeback into glossy, theatrical pop
content.shortHeadline: Ashe makes a theatrical pop return on The Girl of Your Dreams
content.standfirst: After burnout and a stalled career, the singer finds renewed momentum in vintage-styled songs full of strings, big choruses and unabashed melodrama. The review enjoys the confidence, even when the theatrical touches overshoot.

sources.originalTitle: The Girl of Your Dreams

segments.body: Pitchfork’s review traces Ashe’s path from considering retirement to a viral hit with “Stop the Wedding!” and a new album on Atlantic. The record embraces 1970s pop signifiers—operatic flourishes, bright harmonies and piano-led hooks—without disguising how deliberately it borrows from past styles.

segments.title: All in on the show
segments.body: The reviewer finds Ashe most compelling when the record lets its slower songs breathe, while “Swan Lake” and “Sweet Caroline” push their ideas too bluntly. Overall, the album’s unabashed commitment to whimsy and romantic excess comes across as a welcome confidence after years of uncertainty.

content.headline: Shovel Dance Collective makes English folk sound radical again
content.shortHeadline: Shovel Dance Collective finds a present in old folk songs
content.standfirst: On Everything in Readiness, the London group brings archival songs together with drones, field recordings and tape experiments. Its arrangements connect stories of prison and dangerous work to current debates.

sources.originalTitle: Everything in Readiness

segments.body: The nine-piece Shovel Dance Collective treats folk not as a preserved picture of pastoral life but as a record of working people and changing society. On Everything in Readiness, traditional instruments meet electronic distortion, drone and recordings that move between field, church and studio.

segments.title: Songs with present tense
segments.body: The review singles out a pairing of prison songs from 1859 and 1961, whose criticism of incarceration still feels pointed, and a mining song reshaped around unsafe work. The album also brings a previously unrecorded 1694 song, “Bold Captain Avery,” into a contemporary folk collection.

content.headline: Aphex Twin’s Drukqs still bridges the dancefloor and the concert hall
content.shortHeadline: Drukqs at 25: Aphex Twin’s unruly electronic landmark
content.standfirst: A 25th-anniversary edition prompts a reassessment of Richard D. James’s sprawling, once-divisive album. Its prepared piano and extreme rhythms probe the boundary between club music and experimental composition.

sources.originalTitle: Drukqs (25th Anniversary Edition)

segments.body: Pitchfork revisits Drukqs as a record that brings two electronic traditions into uneasy conversation: club music shaped by DJs and dance rhythms, and the experimental lineage of concert-hall composition. Its 100 minutes move between intricate breakbeats, prepared piano and passages that resist any easy genre label.

segments.title: Precision at the edge
segments.body: The review hears the album’s appeal in its tension between control and collapse. Tracks such as “54 Cymru Beats” push rhythm towards noise, while the Disklavier pieces use a digitally programmed piano to turn mechanical precision into something delicate and strange. The length and stylistic leaps remain challenging, but they are part of the album’s argument.

content.headline: One in a Million follows a Syrian family through a decade of change
content.shortHeadline: One in a Million traces a family’s life after displacement
content.standfirst: Itab Azzam and Jack MacInnes’s documentary follows Nisreen, her daughter Israa and their family from flight out of Syria to life in Germany and a return to Aleppo. The film finds liberation and loss unfolding together.

image.caption: Israa in One in a Million.

sources.originalTitle: One in a Million review – deeply moving film about displacement, freedom and the upheaval of starting again

segments.body: Filmed between 2015 and 2025, One in a Million follows Nisreen and her eldest daughter, Israa, across the upheaval of displacement and resettlement. The Guardian review praises the film for avoiding simple roles of refugee as either threat or victim, instead showing how migration changes family relationships from within.

segments.title: Change has a cost
segments.body: As a teenager in Germany, Israa embraces freedoms her father struggles to accept; later, she finds a way back towards her Syrian and Muslim identity and returns to Aleppo. Her father, meanwhile, recognises that his family paid for the loss of status he experienced. The review finds the film’s intimate account of these changes moving, while wishing it had more time to develop them.

content.headline: Blockhead turns a novelist’s insecurity into a comic literary thriller
content.shortHeadline: Blockhead skewers the bad-boy writer myth
content.standfirst: Matt Harlock’s British indie thriller sends a struggling novelist down a grisly road after he meets an imposing builder. The Guardian finds wit and visual invention in its satire of literary machismo.

image.caption: Joe Sims and Danny Horn in Blockhead.

sources.originalTitle: Blockhead review – struggling novelist embraces his inner monster in comic thriller of literary machismo

segments.body: Will Mercer, a novelist struggling to follow his debut, retreats to a friend’s garret and meets Mikey, a charismatic builder who becomes a model for his next work. As Will grows bolder and more violent, writer-director Matt Harlock turns the familiar myth of the dangerous literary bad boy into the target of a comic thriller.

segments.title: A thriller with a sharp eye
segments.body: The review praises Danny Horn’s mix of bravado and insecurity, Joe Sims’s comic deflation of Will’s pretensions, and Harlock’s use of masks, screens and contrasting spaces. It notes a few first-feature stumbles but finds the film’s satire and cinematic confidence effective.

content.headline: Why (500) Days of Summer remains one writer’s feelgood film
content.shortHeadline: (500) Days of Summer, revisited every year
content.standfirst: A first date turned into a marriage, and an annual rewatch of the film that accompanied it. The Guardian writer returns to its open-ended romance to reconsider what Tom and Summer owe each other.

image.caption: Joseph Gordon-Levitt and Zooey Deschanel in (500) Days of Summer.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Funny and self-aware’: why (500) Days of Summer is my feelgood movie

segments.body: The writer first saw (500) Days of Summer on a date in 2009; the couple later married and still revisit it each year. Its shifting timeline, indie-pop soundtrack and Los Angeles setting remain part of the appeal, but the film’s lasting hold lies in the questions it leaves open about Tom and Summer’s relationship.

segments.title: A story that changes with the viewer
segments.body: Each rewatch invites a different reading: is Tom romantic or naïve, and is Summer setting a boundary or dismissing his feelings? The writer describes the film as sympathetic to Tom without forcing a verdict, making it a useful lens through which to revisit the couple’s own ideas about love.

content.headline: Rhys Ifans and Laura Linney find humour in a Parkinson’s drama
content.shortHeadline: Onwards and Sideways puts Parkinson’s in the frame
content.standfirst: The actors discuss a BBC film written by Paul Mayhew-Archer, who lives with the condition. Research with people with Parkinson’s shaped their performances and helped the production approach a highly individual illness with care.

image.caption: Rhys Ifans and Laura Linney in Onwards and Sideways.

sources.originalTitle: ‘We both know how we feel about death and dying’: Rhys Ifans and Laura Linney on their brutally honest Parkinson’s drama

segments.body: Onwards and Sideways brings together two characters diagnosed with Parkinson’s, played by Rhys Ifans and Laura Linney, in a story that mixes difficult realities with humour. Writer Paul Mayhew-Archer drew on his own experience of the condition, and Ifans says that combination of comedy and devastation first drew him to the project.

segments.title: Learning the condition’s language
segments.body: Linney and Ifans worked with people who support Parkinson’s patients, including dance groups, to understand its varied physical effects. They describe trying to translate that knowledge into performance without implying that everyone experiences the condition in the same way. The film opens in UK cinemas on 6 November.

content.headline: I Died honours Tzotzil women confronting patriarchal violence
content.shortHeadline: I Died finds resilience in the lives of Tzotzil women
content.standfirst: Ana Ts’uyeb’s documentary follows three generations of women in her Mexican highland village as they recall abuse and lost opportunities. Its intimate images of work and land give the film its quiet force.

image.caption: A still from Ana Ts’uyeb’s documentary I Died.

sources.originalTitle: I Died review – moving portrait of Tzotzil women confronting patriarchal violence in the Mexican highlands

segments.body: I Died centres on Ts’uyeb’s mother, aunt and sister-in-law, women from different generations who describe education and ambitions blocked by male relatives, alongside physical and psychological abuse. The Guardian review notes how matter-of-factly they recount experiences that appear common in their community.

segments.title: Everyday work, a different future
segments.body: Rather than relying on sit-down interviews, Ts’uyeb films the women weaving, harvesting and carrying out daily tasks, creating a visual record of their customs as well as their resilience. The review says the film offers little background on Zapatista land activism, but finds its attention to the women’s lives emotionally powerful.

content.headline: Fourteen box-office flops that deserve another look
content.shortHeadline: The films that failed at the box office but reward a revisit
content.standfirst: From The Thing and Dune to Babylon and Furiosa, this guide argues that commercial failure need not settle a film’s reputation. It revisits ambitious projects that found appreciation after their initial release.

sources.originalTitle: The 14 spectacular film flops that are actually worth watching

segments.body: The i Paper’s selection takes in films that were financial disappointments or critical misfires on release but have since earned a second look. Its examples range from John Carpenter’s The Thing and David Lynch’s Dune to more recent, ambitious films such as Cloud Atlas and Babylon.

segments.title: A case for reconsideration
segments.body: The article suggests that timing, tone and expectation can shape a film’s fate as much as its merits: The Thing arrived amid demand for feelgood blockbusters, while Last Action Hero opened against Jurassic Park. The picks make the case for reappraisal rather than treating box-office performance as a final verdict.

content.headline: Oasis reunion documentary captures the euphoria but skips the hard questions
content.shortHeadline: Oasis reunion film thrills, but leaves the story unfinished
content.standfirst: Steven Knight’s documentary finds the global joy of Oasis’s comeback tour, from Cardiff to South America and South Korea. Its account of reconciliation, however, leaves the brothers’ long estrangement largely unexplained.

image.caption: A still from Steven Knight’s Oasis documentary.

sources.originalTitle: Oasis fans’ most important question remains unanswered

segments.body: Don’t Look Back in Anger follows Oasis around the world in 2025, capturing the scale of the reunion and the devotion of fans who have carried the band’s songs across generations. The i Paper review praises the concert footage and the feeling of shared excitement, especially in scenes from the tour’s Cardiff opening night.

segments.title: The reconciliation remains offscreen
segments.body: The film moves from a brief history of the band’s split to rehearsals, leaving the negotiations and family history behind the reunion unexplored. It also omits the dynamic-ticketing controversy. The review finds the brothers’ evident warmth touching, but says the film’s message of forgiveness is less convincing without showing how it came about.

content.headline: November’s film guide ranges from Ian Charleson to The Hunger Games
content.shortHeadline: November films: Elsinore, Hunger Games and more
content.standfirst: BBC Culture’s monthly guide picks out new releases and streaming titles, including Andrew Scott as actor Ian Charleson, a new Hunger Games prequel and a drama about disability-rights activist Judith Heumann.

sources.originalTitle: Elsinore to The Hunger Games: 12 of the best films to watch in November

segments.body: Among the month’s releases, BBC Culture highlights Elsinore, with Andrew Scott playing Ian Charleson as he takes on Hamlet while seriously ill, and Sunrise on the Reaping, another expansion of The Hunger Games world. The guide also includes Being Heumann, based on the disability-rights activist’s account of the 1977 occupation of a San Francisco federal building.

segments.title: From intimate drama to spectacle
segments.body: The list ranges from Jordan Firstman’s Club Kid, a comedy about a New York party promoter who discovers he has a son, to the crime story The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, directed by David Fincher from a Quentin Tarantino script. Each entry includes release dates and selected critical responses.

content.headline: Blue Planet III review: Attenborough’s ocean series still finds wonders
content.shortHeadline: Blue Planet III is a vivid return to the ocean
content.standfirst: The new series uncovers animal behaviour with the help of remote cameras, from dolphins using sea sponges to sharks hunting in packs. Its account of a heat-damaged reef also carries a forceful conservation appeal.

image.caption: Three rough-toothed dolphins swim in the open ocean in Blue Planet III.

sources.originalTitle: Blue Planet III review – David Attenborough makes another absolute corker

segments.body: The Guardian review argues that Blue Planet III need not match the landmark status of its predecessors to succeed. Its opening episode brings fresh discoveries, including dolphins using sea sponges and tawny sharks working together to drive fish towards shore.

segments.title: Wonder and warning
segments.body: The series balances comic animal behaviour with an unsettling account of a heatwave killing an anemone and damaging its reef. David Attenborough ends with a plea to protect the natural world, delivered, the reviewer notes, in a voice now almost a whisper.

content.headline: Million Pound Shot used a fake gameshow to expose gambling tactics
content.shortHeadline: Million Pound Shot’s hoax turns a quiz into a warning
content.standfirst: The Channel 4 pilot was a staged experiment: contestants and the floor manager were actors, while the studio audience was unaware. Its lesson focused on how betting mechanics can make losses feel abstract and encourage people to keep playing.

image.caption: An illustration of the blurred reality staged in Million Pound Shot.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I can’t afford to lose £3,000’: the ‘gameshow’ that made contestants gamble their own money

segments.body: Bradley Walsh’s Million Pound Shot appeared to be a gameshow where contestants risked their own money, but the programme was a hoax designed to highlight gambling-industry tactics. Its staged players were actors; the studio audience was not told it was watching an experiment.

segments.title: The mechanics of keeping people in the game
segments.body: The programme uses a contestant’s escalating losses and a free bet to demonstrate how abstract “bet balls” and an apparent chance to recover can encourage further play. Psychologist Steve Sharman and campaigner Will Prochaska explain the tactics; the report also includes responses from gambling companies and the Betting and Gaming Council, which dispute some of the criticism.

content.headline: Yaga review: Hudson Williams leads a witchy mystery with a feminist twist
content.shortHeadline: Yaga’s folk-horror mystery gets stranger as it unfolds
content.standfirst: The Heated Rivalry actor plays lookalikes in a Canadian coastal-town mystery inspired by the Baba Yaga legend. The Guardian finds it uneven but increasingly rewarding as its supernatural and feminist strands come together.

image.caption: Hudson Williams in Yaga.

sources.originalTitle: Yaga review – this erotic witchy thriller starring Hudson Williams is a total head-messer

segments.body: Hudson Williams plays missing heir Henry Park and his lookalike roommate Logan in Yaga, a mystery that sends private investigator Charlie Rapp and police officer Carson searching a foggy Canadian town. The review describes a steadily accumulating mix of clues, eerie images and deliberately odd characters.

segments.title: A strange story finds its footing
segments.body: The Guardian finds the series hit-and-miss, with a slow build and some distractions, but says it strengthens as its ominous atmosphere gives way to a more procedural investigation. Its feminist reworking of the Baba Yaga legend helps the show become more compelling, though the reviewer leaves its exact appeal unresolved.

content.headline: Strictly’s Halloween triple dance-off sends Lawrence Robb home
content.shortHeadline: Strictly’s triple dance-off ends Lawrence Robb’s run
content.standfirst: Lawrence Robb and partner Jowita Przystał left after the first three-couple dance-off, while Graeme Hall and Tabby Stoecker were saved by viewers. The Guardian’s live coverage also records complaints about the format and judging.

image.caption: Vito Coppola and Lacey Turner.

sources.originalTitle: Strictly Come Dancing Halloween special results – as it happened

segments.body: Emmerdale actor Lawrence Robb became the fifth celebrity eliminated from Strictly Come Dancing 2026 after the Halloween results show’s first triple dance-off. The Guardian’s live coverage reports that Graeme Hall and Tabby Stoecker, both at the bottom of the leaderboard, escaped the dance-off through viewer votes.

segments.title: A format viewers questioned
segments.body: The coverage notes audience objections to putting three couples into the dance-off and limiting safe contestants’ chance to speak. It also questions head judge Shirley Ballas’s uneven scoring, while acknowledging that Robb’s record across the series made his exit difficult to dispute.

content.headline: Black Doves and Stick lead this week’s streaming picks
content.shortHeadline: What to stream: Black Doves, Stick and Muhammad Ali
content.standfirst: The Guardian’s guide includes the return of Keira Knightley’s spy thriller and Owen Wilson’s golf comedy, alongside a drama about Muhammad Ali’s early life and several documentary and crime picks.

image.caption: Ambika Mod and Keira Knightley in Black Doves.

sources.originalTitle: Black Doves to Stick: the seven best shows to stream this week

segments.body: Black Doves returns with Helen Webb still balancing political proximity and espionage, while the second season of Stick follows Owen Wilson’s golf pro as his protégé begins to outgrow him. The Guardian guide recommends the former for its chaotic spy-family plotting and the latter for Wilson’s vulnerability beneath the comedy.

segments.title: More to queue up
segments.body: Other picks include The Greatest, a drama about Muhammad Ali’s childhood and early career, and a documentary about the Canadian sketch show Second City TV. The list also flags a new mother-and-son thriller and a camp legal drama, with UK and international streaming dates supplied.

content.headline: The Gilded Age returns as old money faces new rivals
content.shortHeadline: The Gilded Age returns to glossy social plotting
content.standfirst: The Guardian’s evening guide picks out the period drama’s return, with Agnes seeking to defend her standing as new wealth challenges the old order. The same listings also flag documentaries and a legal drama.

image.caption: A scene from The Gilded Age.

sources.originalTitle: TV tonight: The Gilded Age returns in all its glossy Julian Fellowes’ glory

segments.body: In The Gilded Age’s return, Agnes plots to hold on to her place in society as the newly rich George and Bertha Russell remain at the centre of the drama. The Guardian’s listing describes the show as a glossy period confection that has embraced its own lightness, while noting the modern resonance of old money facing ambitious new power.

segments.title: Other viewing tonight
segments.body: The guide also recommends the conclusion of a documentary about the expulsion of Uganda’s Asian population in 1972, the latest episode of David Harewood’s legal drama, and a Dispatches film following Afghans in exile trying to rescue relatives from Taliban rule.

content.headline: Celebrity Traitors finale surprises, but critics differ on the season
content.shortHeadline: Celebrity Traitors ends with a shock—and split verdicts
content.standfirst: Bash’s late deduction sent the prize to the Faithfuls’ charities after Maya and Kenny were exposed. Three i Paper accounts celebrate the finale’s turnaround but disagree over whether the season’s problems lay in its format or James Acaster’s reluctant play.

image.caption: The Endgame Round Table in The Celebrity Traitors.

sources.originalTitle: One player’s lack of ego saved Celebrity Traitors
James Acaster was stitched up
James Acaster has made a mockery of The Celebrity Traitors

segments.body: The Celebrity Traitors finale saw Maya Jama banished before Bash worked out that Kenny was the last Traitor. His vote persuaded Romesh Ranganathan to change sides, giving the Faithfuls’ charities £83,000. The i Paper review credits Bash’s lack of ego with delivering a late surprise after a series that had seemed headed for a predictable Traitor win.

segments.title: Where did the season go wrong?
segments.body: The i Paper’s other accounts disagree about the cause of the season’s unevenness. One blames early format choices—including Richard E Grant’s accidental confession and James Acaster’s forced recruitment—for destabilising the game; another argues that Acaster’s decision to confess removed tension just as the Faithful were closing in. The finale’s payoff did not erase the debate.

perspectives.body: The i Paper’s structural critique argues that the early forced recruitment and rapid loss of Traitors made this season feel unstable before its finale.

content.headline: Doctor Who’s uncertain future leaves fans waiting for a return
content.shortHeadline: Doctor Who is on pause, and fans want it back
content.standfirst: With no new Doctor announced, a cancelled Christmas special and the end of its Disney+ partnership, the BBC series faces an open-ended pause. Fans and former writers debate what went wrong and what a revival should preserve.

image.caption: Several actors who have played the Doctor, including Peter Capaldi, David Tennant and Jodie Whittaker.

sources.originalTitle: The sad, slow death of Doctor Who

segments.body: Doctor Who has been off air since its 2025 series, and the BBC has ended its collaboration with Disney+ without a replacement partner yet in place. A planned Christmas special has been cancelled, and there is no Doctor currently attached to the next instalment.

segments.title: A changing institution
segments.body: Fans and people who have worked on the series point to its history of reinvention, from its 2005 revival to more recent changes in cast and showrunner. They differ on the reasons for declining viewing figures, but stress the show’s enduring values of kindness and curiosity—and the risk of letting it become only an archive.

content.headline: Elden Ring’s film adaptation faces the challenge of making its world matter
content.shortHeadline: Can Elden Ring’s film make its vast world compelling?
content.standfirst: Alex Garland’s adaptation has been shot and is reportedly in post-production, with a budget said to approach $200m. The Guardian argues that spectacle alone will not solve the challenge of turning the game’s brutal world into a compelling film.

image.caption: A scene from Elden Ring.

sources.originalTitle: Alex Garland’s Elden Ring adaptation is on course to be Hollywood’s goriest ever fantasy movie

segments.body: Elden Ring has sold more than 30 million copies, and its film adaptation, written and directed by Alex Garland, is reportedly in post-production. The Guardian notes the scale of the project, its high-profile cast and the reported budget, while asking how a film can give audiences more than an explanation of the game’s mythology.

segments.title: More than a world to explore
segments.body: The article compares the project with fantasy adaptations that struggled to translate vast source material into engaging stories. Elden Ring’s creatures and body horror also distinguish it from more familiar Hollywood fantasy, while Garland’s history of resisting reassuring endings leaves open how much freedom he will have with a production of this scale.

content.headline: Night Plane turns a flight-attendant job sim into existential horror
content.shortHeadline: Night Plane sends a flight attendant into horror
content.standfirst: Liquid Static Studio’s retro-style indie game begins with airport routines before twisting into a journey through demons, strange lounges and a crashed plane. The Guardian finds its mix of humour and genuinely unsettling imagery effective.

image.caption: A scene from Night Plane.

sources.originalTitle: Night Plane review – join the jumbo jet to hell in this indie horror head trip

segments.body: In Night Plane, the player checks in passengers and serves a flight before a crash sends them back to the airport, where some travellers are demons in disguise. The Guardian review places it in a growing strain of horror built around repetitive workplace simulations and finds the shift from routine to nightmare absorbing.

segments.title: The uncanny on a budget
segments.body: Low-poly visuals evoke the original PlayStation era, while flickering lights, strange voices and recurring images of wreckage pull the game towards existential horror. Its dry comedy keeps the early sections playful, but the review says the imagery eventually becomes genuinely disturbing. A run takes around four or five hours, with further quests and endings to discover.

content.headline: AI-assisted game mods are getting easier—and harder to contain
content.shortHeadline: AI is changing how game mods are made
content.standfirst: Tools that can help decompile game code have lowered the technical barrier to building mashups, from browser experiments to console emulation. The Guardian examines the creative, legal and commercial consequences.

image.caption: A video-game mashup shown on social media.

sources.originalTitle: Social media is full of weird video game mashups. Where are they all coming from?

segments.body: The Guardian’s account traces a wave of social-media game mashups to AI-assisted coding tools that can make decompiling a game’s code far quicker. The writer says a simple browser-game experiment took minutes, while more ambitious projects still need human input and technical adjustment.

segments.title: A new scale of access
segments.body: The article describes the ease of creating mods and accessing emulated games as a potential challenge for publishers, particularly where copyright is involved. It asks whether AI companies will face pressure to limit tools built on creative work, while noting that claims of piracy and access are already being argued over by players.

content.headline: Eight indie horror games offer fresh scares for Halloween
content.shortHeadline: Eight indie horror games for a Halloween night
content.standfirst: The Guardian’s guide ranges from a dark fairytale adventure to a Scottish Gaelic takeaway horror and a card game against the devil. Its picks show how inventive small-scale horror has become.

image.caption: A scene from The Killing Stone.

sources.originalTitle: Eight great new indie horror games for Halloween

segments.body: The guide recommends eight recent independent horror games across several styles. Allogloom uses point-and-click fairytale imagery, while one short game puts players to work in a Scottish takeaway where a suspicious new dish comes from the cellar.

segments.title: From the occult to the uncanny
segments.body: Other selections include a 17th-century witch-hunt adventure, The Killing Stone’s card game against the devil, and Night Plane’s retro air-travel nightmare. The roundup also includes Hellraiser: Revival, Antarctic cosmic horror seen through a penguin’s eyes, and two puzzle-led mysteries.

content.headline: Ice loss could be permanent even if global temperatures fall back
content.shortHeadline: A climate overshoot could cause lasting ice loss
content.standfirst: A UN-backed report warns that even a temporary rise above the Paris 1.5C threshold could leave lasting damage to glaciers, sea ice and polar ice sheets. The authors say temperatures need to return well below that level over time.

image.caption: Ice sheets covering Greenland and Antarctica are melting faster than in the 1990s.

sources.originalTitle: Cryosphere faces permanent damage when world overshoots 1.5C, scientists warn

segments.body: A report by 80 scientists convened by the International Cryosphere Climate Initiative and the UN Environment Programme warns that temporary overshoot of the Paris agreement’s 1.5C warming limit could cause widespread, lasting damage to Earth’s ice and snow. Some systems could take centuries or millennia to recover, even if temperatures later fall.

segments.title: Risks across the ice
segments.body: The report says current policies could lead to peak warming of about 2.8C, with nearly all near-surface permafrost thawing and severe disruption to ocean circulation becoming likely. Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets are already losing ice about six times faster than in the 1990s, and the authors say they would keep losing mass even if temperatures returned to 1.5C.

The consequences reach beyond the polar regions. The report estimates that glaciers would retain less of their current ice under current policies than if warming were limited to 1.5C; in the Hindu Kush Himalayas, a major water source, it projects 41% of ice mass would remain under current policies, compared with 83% at 1.5C. These are projections, not a timetable for specific local impacts.

content.headline: Medical micro-robots are moving from gut drug delivery towards blood vessels
content.shortHeadline: Micro-robots aim to deliver drugs with greater precision
content.standfirst: Swallowable capsules already let doctors inspect the gut, while experimental magnetic devices are being tested for targeted drug delivery. The work is promising, but most applications remain at an early stage.

image.caption: Illustration of a micro-robot being developed to deliver drugs in the gut.

sources.originalTitle: The astonishing micro-robots you swallow that spot cancer and might help treat it

segments.body: Medical micro-robots are being developed to deliver drugs to specific parts of the body. A Beijing team reported testing a 6.5mm magnetic device in pigs: it travelled to the lower intestine and released insulin there. The result is an animal study, not evidence that the device is ready for patients.

segments.title: From cameras to targeted treatment
segments.body: Swallowable camera capsules are already used to investigate gut problems, and some can be steered around the stomach using magnets. Researchers are working on more complex devices that could deliver medication locally, potentially reducing the amount needed elsewhere in the body. That possible benefit is still under investigation.

segments.title: Earlier-stage possibilities
segments.body: Researchers have also demonstrated a 2mm magnetic robot moving through a pig’s bloodstream, and a separate test used one to deliver a clot-dissolving drug in a model of the brain’s circulation. The article says devices small enough to travel through blood vessels are probably at least a decade from patient use; other proposed applications, including treating tumours, are experimental.

content.headline: Scientists warn bird flu in Utah mink could create new risks
content.shortHeadline: Bird flu in mink raises concern about viral mixing
content.standfirst: An outbreak on a Utah fur farm has raised concern because mink can carry both bird and human flu viruses. Experts warn that mixing could create new strains, but the reporting does not say that the virus is spreading between people.

image.caption: Mink on fur farms may provide an environment for flu viruses to mix.

sources.originalTitle: Bird flu is one mutation from serious risk to humans – how prepared is the UK?

segments.body: Mink on a Utah fur farm have been dying from bird flu in an outbreak reported to have been under way since at least August. Scientists are concerned because mink are mammals with respiratory systems similar to those of humans, and can harbour both bird and human flu strains.

segments.title: A risk, not a prediction
segments.body: Researchers say different flu strains could swap genetic material in an infected animal, a process known as reassortment. An infected farm worker who also had seasonal flu could be another route for the viruses to mix, experts warn. The article says the bird flu strain has not appeared to spread easily from person to person; the possibility of a new strain is a concern, not an established outcome.

segments.title: Preparedness questions
segments.body: The UK Health Security Agency says it has systems to detect human cases of avian flu and is ready to respond if needed. Experts interviewed by the i Paper also point to practical preparation: suitable tests and faster vaccine development. One expert argues that researchers should test how quickly they can make a bird-flu lateral-flow test.

content.headline: Sea-level rise reshaped the land around Venice over 10,000 years
content.shortHeadline: Venice lagoon was once dry land, study finds
content.standfirst: Seismic data and sediment cores reveal that the present-day lagoon once extended far inland. The reconstruction traces rapid, uneven sea-level rise and the changing landscapes in which people lived.

sources.originalTitle: How rising seas transformed dry land into Venice lagoon

segments.body: The present-day Venice lagoon was once dry land extending more than 30 miles from the coast, according to research reconstructing the northern Adriatic over the past 10,000 years. The study combined seismic data with sediment cores from coastal basins in northern Italy, Slovenia and northern Croatia.

The researchers describe sea levels rising in fits and starts from just over 10,000 years ago, at times by as much as 25mm a year. The changes transformed the coastline and meant Mesolithic hunter-gatherers had to adapt their hunting and fishing. The landscape later became more stable, helping settlements and farming develop.

content.headline: Cyberattacks on supermarket cooling systems disrupt stores across Europe
content.shortHeadline: A new wave of attacks hits supermarket freezers
content.standfirst: Retailers in several European countries reported refrigeration failures, spoiled goods and disrupted shelves. The incidents follow an earlier attack in France, renewing questions about the security of internet-connected systems that control food storage.

image.caption: A worker removes spoiled goods after cooling units overheated at a Swedish supermarket.

sources.originalTitle: Supermarket freezers across Europe hit by second suspected cyber-attack
More European supermarkets are getting their freezers hacked
A fresh wave of cyberattacks has hit Europe’s supermarket refrigerators, destroying food across countries

segments.body: Supermarkets in at least seven European countries reported refrigeration problems after cooling units were tampered with or temperatures rose overnight. Several chains confirmed cyberattacks. Some stores removed chilled and frozen goods from sale, while retailers reported disruption across Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Finland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden.

segments.title: Connected systems, physical consequences
segments.body: The incidents follow an attack in France last month in which hackers reportedly changed settings on refrigerators at hundreds of supermarkets, causing food losses. Modern cooling systems can be monitored and controlled remotely, making them useful for maintenance but also exposing them to cyber risks. Authorities have not identified who was behind the attacks.

perspectives.body: TechCrunch reports that researchers had warned months earlier that some Danfoss refrigeration units were vulnerable to remote attacks. It also notes that a previous cyberattack on a US food distributor caused shortages, underscoring how digital weaknesses can reach beyond individual stores.

content.headline: NHS claims about Palantir benefits challenged by 29 hospital trusts
content.shortHeadline: Trusts dispute NHS claims about Palantir system use
content.standfirst: Freedom of information responses suggest some trusts listed as benefiting from the data platform say it is not live or its applications are not in use. NHS England says its benefits figures include different kinds of activity.

image.caption: The trusts told the Guardian the platform was not live or its applications were not in use.

sources.originalTitle: Palantir AI tech unused or little used by 29 NHS trusts said to be benefiting from it

segments.body: Twenty-nine hospital trusts that NHS England lists as “realising benefits” from Palantir’s £330m Federated Data Platform told the Guardian that the system was not live or that they were not using its applications. The findings came from more than 100 freedom of information requests. NHS England separately says 137 trusts are live with the platform.

segments.title: What counts as a benefit?
segments.body: NHS England says nearly 140 trusts have reported benefits from tools on the platform. It has previously said these can include back-office analysis and data submission, not only applications directly supporting patient care. One trust, for example, said it was not operationally using the platform while NHS England counted it as live because infrastructure was in place for data submission.

segments.title: Questions over evidence
segments.body: The Guardian reports that NHS England has claimed trusts using the platform carried out 117,539 more operations in a year, but the agency has conceded it cannot prove cause and effect. A statistics watchdog is taking forward the issue under its casework function. Critics are calling for transparent, verifiable reporting; Palantir says its software is helping improve care and hospital operations.

content.headline: Data-centre opposition becomes an issue in Maine and Florida races
content.shortHeadline: Data centres enter US election debates in Maine and Florida
content.standfirst: Campaigns in two states are confronting local concerns about data centres, including power, water, jobs and community control. Candidates’ positions differ, while the reporting also traces the role of technology money in the races.

sources.originalTitle: Maine’s data center revolt will decide who controls the Senate
Could data center backlash flip Florida?

segments.body: Data-centre development has become a campaign issue in Maine and Florida, where residents have raised concerns about local resources and who benefits from new projects. A poll cited by The Verge found 76% of surveyed Mainers opposed building a data centre in their community; a separate Florida poll cited in its reporting found 68% opposed.

segments.title: Different races, similar questions
segments.body: In Maine’s Senate contest, candidates have faced questions about development, electricity costs and promised jobs. In Florida’s governor’s race, Democrat David Jolly has proposed a one-year moratorium, while Republican Byron Donalds has supported welcoming the industry and says local governments decide whether projects proceed. Some Florida residents interviewed by The Verge say the issue could affect how they vote.

segments.title: Local benefits under scrutiny
